reader_summary:
This section explains how feedback changes the chance of choosing an answer. Action 0 means answer 3 and action 1 means answer 4. Both start at probability 0.5. Reward 1 minus baseline 0.5 gives advantage 0.5, so minimizing the displayed negative-advantage-times-log-probability objective favors the selected answer 4. Subtracting 0.1 times the calculated gradient [0.25,-0.25] gives scores [-0.025,0.025] and probabilities [0.487503,0.512497]. I can follow why the probability gain is smaller than the score gain and why one successful update does not guarantee correctness. Changing reward to 0 makes the same action worse than its reference and reverses the direction.

The later experiment describes a separate finite-action policy: three one-hot encoded integers produce 18 input entries, then 48 intermediate entries and scores for 17 answer actions. It really samples and updates weights, whereas the tiny code fixes its action and updates only two scores. I can distinguish training reward from strict success on new questions: the strict branch has a reported final training batch 39/64 but no new-question successes, and the weak branch chooses the all-numbers action for all 384 new-question samples. Those are cited experimental results, not runs I reproduced. The denominators are made explicit: 24 distinct questions, 16 samples each, 384 sampled actions, and 1,200 batches times 64 actions equals 76,800 training samples.

background_and_links.details: I followed the explicit C.7 links for reward, log/probability, gradient updates, linear mixing and AdamW, then only necessary onward links for tensor/indexing, concrete softmax and the token/two-language-model references. These supplied the needed meanings without searching unrelated source. The direct C.7 link to C.5 makes it clear that spending extra computation on an answer can keep weights fixed, whereas the update example changes scores and the finite policy training changes weights. C.6 supplies why enumerating every number defeats the weak proxy but fails the required single-answer task. I did not need C.2, 5.10, the other optimizer prerequisites, or the optional W.1/T.1 environment instructions for the bounded calculation; the optional replay remains unexecuted.

terminology.details: Policy is the answer probability distribution; reward is the verifier feedback; baseline is a reference rather than a true answer; advantage is reward minus that reference. RLVR is expanded, REINFORCE is described as estimating an update from actually sampled actions, one-hot is concretely illustrated, and entropy is explained by uniform versus concentrated action probabilities. W.3 supplies tensor and axes, W.4 and 1.7 supply natural log and softmax, W.6 supplies gradient/backward/no_grad, and 5.4/5.5 explain AdamW history and separate decay. In the finite policy, effective_tokens=0 is understandable as no generated text fragments, while sampled_actions counts chosen predefined outputs. Autoregressive generation is interpretable using C.5’s description of deciding successive text fragments from prior content. The few unresolved labels and the compact Python syntax are recorded as nonblocking issues.

examples.details: I can track the two actions and every important numeric transition. At the starting p(action 1)=0.5 and advantage=0.5, the displayed loss is -0.5 log(0.5), about 0.346574 by the formula; the code does not print that loss. The gradient is [0.25,-0.25], so subtracting 0.1 times it gives [-0.025,0.025]. Softmax converts these shared scores to [0.487503,0.512497], rather than adding 0.025 directly to a probability. The formal policy input length is 3 times 6=18; it scores single answers 0 through 15 and one enumeration answer, 17 actions in all. The baseline smoothing weights 0.95 and 0.05 keep most old reference and add a little current batch reward for the next batch. Subtracting 0.005 times entropy from the training cost favors a more spread distribution but does not guarantee a correct action. The highest-probability and sample columns have different denominators, and the (0+3)+3 example makes a confidently chosen wrong answer concrete. I read the cited training/evaluation outcomes as claims in the text, without reproducing them.

program_explanation.details: There are two fenced blocks. In the Python block, logits stores two adjustable scores with gradient tracking. Action 1 selects answer 4. reward and baseline are fixed Python numbers, so no derivative is taken through a verifier. detach makes the before comparison independent of gradient tracking; softmax(0) operates over the single two-candidate axis, rather than selecting candidate 0. log_softmax(0)[action] obtains the selected action’s log probability. backward computes the loss sensitivities into logits.grad. In no_grad, updated is a new tensor calculated by subtracting the step times the gradient, and after converts these updated scores to probabilities. tolist exposes values for printing, and the final compact expression rounds each probability. I ran the unchanged Python fence in an existing .venv CPU process and captured all four printed lines; the results match the predicted gradient, scores and before/after distributions, allowing ordinary floating-point digits in the scores. The bash block sets up local Git LFS, requests the named public asset, then invokes the reasoning experiment entry point using CPU. Its outputs path and warning that policy files differ from TinyLM weights are explicit. I read that block but did not run its installation, download or training commands.

exercise.details: The change is precisely reward=0.0 with baseline=0.5 and action=1 unchanged. I saved the prediction before running it: advantage=-0.5, gradient=[-0.25,0.25], new scores=[0.025,-0.025], and after probabilities=[0.512497,0.487503]. The captured CPU run gives those results. The direction follows being worse than the reference; a nonnegative reward alone does not imply a probability increase. The objective here can be negative when advantage is negative, as its displayed formula permits; the four printed results are sufficient to check the requested direction.
